finding.claim: deleteAccount calls canDelete() but discards the boolean result, so the authorization check is never enforced. Any caller can delete any account (broken access control / IDOR). closeAccount correctly uses assertCanDelete, which shows the intended pattern.
finding.source: Any authenticated user calling DELETE /accounts/{id} with an arbitrary account id
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at line 23, which deletes the account

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) is the entry point for DELETE /accounts/{id}; id is attacker-controlled
Account looked up by id with no ownership scoping
canDelete(u, a) returns a boolean that is ignored, so there is no throw and no early return

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is canDelete at line 22, and its result is unused. assertCanDelete is not called on this path. No other auth layer exists in the repo, such as a filter or annotation. Compare closeAccount at line 29, which does enforce the check.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (line 9-11) returns a boolean, but its result is discarded at line 22; assertCanDelete (which throws) is not called in deleteAccount. No filter/annotation or other auth layer exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: src/AccountService.java:22 calls canDelete(u, a) as a bare statement with the result discarded, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated non-owner, non-admin user, unlike closeAccount at line 29 which uses the throwing assertCanDelete.

verdict_facts.guard_found: canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) returns a boolean, but deleteAccount calls it as a bare statement at line 22 and discards the result. assertCanDelete, which throws, is not called on this path. No other filter or annotation exists.
verdict_facts.reason: AccountService.java:22 discards the boolean from canDelete, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated user, whereas closeAccount enforces the check with the throwing assertCanDelete at line 29.
